mcqs.q: How much even space should an impression tray provide for the impression material?
opts: 2–3 mm
1–2 mm
4–5 mm
5–6 mm
mcqs.explain: An even layer of this thickness shrinks evenly; a thick, uneven bulk shrinks unpredictably.

mcqs.q: How far apical to the gingival margins should the tray be extended?
opts: 3–5 mm
1–2 mm
6–8 mm
Exactly to the gingival margin
mcqs.explain: The tray must include all prepared AND unprepared teeth, with this extension beyond the margins.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the ideal requirements of an impression tray?
opts: It must be flexible so it can be removed past undercuts
It must be rigid
It must be dimensionally stable
It must be retentive for the impression material
mcqs.explain: A flexible tray rebounds after removal and distorts the impression — rigidity is the first requirement.

mcqs.q: Retention of the impression material to the tray may be:
opts: Mechanical or chemical
Mechanical only
Chemical only
Neither — the material is held by the undercuts of the teeth
mcqs.explain: Perforations and rim-lock give mechanical retention; tray adhesive gives chemical retention.

mcqs.q: The four viscosities of impression material are putty, heavy body, light body and:
opts: Medium body
Extra light body
Monophase
Very heavy body
mcqs.explain: Medium body is the viscosity used alone in the single mix technique.

mcqs.q: In manual mixing, the endpoint is a mix that is:
opts: Homogeneous — free from streaks
Slightly streaked, to confirm both components are present
Stiff enough to hold its shape on the spatula
Warm to the touch
mcqs.explain: Remaining streaks mean the reaction will be incomplete in those areas.

mcqs.q: In machine mixing, the material is supplied as:
opts: Prepackaged cartridges with a disposable mixing tip attached to the mixing tube
Powder and liquid in bulk containers
Pre-weighed capsules for an amalgamator
Single-paste syringes activated by light
mcqs.explain: The tip mixes the two components as they are extruded.

mcqs.q: Which is an ADVANTAGE of machine mixing?
opts: A homogeneous mix with fewer voids
Less waste material than hand mixing
It requires a less steady hand than hand mixing
It costs less than hand mixing
mcqs.explain: More waste and the need for a steadier hand with larger gun systems are the listed disadvantages.

mcqs.q: Larger gun systems require a steadier hand because:
opts: The margin of the preparation must be tracked precisely
The cartridge is heavier than the tooth
The material sets faster in a large cartridge
The tip is shorter than on a small system
mcqs.explain: Any wobble while injecting leaves the margin incompletely covered.

mcqs.q: The three impression techniques listed are one step, putty wash, and:
opts: Single mix
Triple mix
Reversible hydrocolloid
Closed mouth
mcqs.explain: The closed-mouth triple technique is presented separately, after the three.

mcqs.q: The single mix technique uses medium body and is indicated:
opts: For implants only
For all crown preparations
For edentulous arches only
For bite registration only
mcqs.explain: An implant impression records a rigid coping rather than a fragile margin, so one viscosity suffices.

mcqs.q: The double mix impression uses:
opts: Two different viscosities — putty or heavy body with light body
Two separate trays
Two mixing methods in sequence
Two different materials, one silicone and one polyether
mcqs.explain: It may be performed as a one-step or a two-step procedure.

mcqs.q: Which type of tray is used in the ONE-STEP technique?
opts: A custom tray
A stock tray
A dual-arch tray
No tray
mcqs.explain: The putty wash technique uses a stock tray, since the putty itself forms the custom-fitting carrier.

mcqs.q: In the one-step technique, when is tray adhesive applied?
opts: After evaluating the custom tray in the mouth, before isolating the teeth
After the retraction cord has been removed
After loading the tray with heavy body
It is not used in the one-step technique
mcqs.explain: The sequence is: evaluate the tray, apply adhesive, isolate and place cord, then dispense the material.

mcqs.q: In step 4 of the one-step technique, the base and catalyst are dispensed:
opts: In equal amounts, on SEPARATE pads
In equal amounts, on the same pad
In a 2:1 ratio on the same pad
Directly into the tray
mcqs.explain: Separate pads are needed because the light body and heavy body are being prepared at the same time.

mcqs.q: In the one-step technique, the heavy body is mixed:
opts: At the same time as the light body
Only after the light body has been injected
Before the retraction cord is placed
After the tray has been seated
mcqs.explain: Both must still be unset when the tray is seated so that they bond into a single body.

mcqs.q: In the one-step technique, when is the retraction cord removed?
opts: After the materials are mixed, immediately before injecting the light body
Before the tray adhesive is applied
After the tray has been seated
It is left in place within the impression
mcqs.explain: The teeth are then washed and dried before the light body is injected.

mcqs.q: After seating the tray in the one-step technique, the operator should:
opts: Hold it in place for the complete setting time
Release it as soon as the patient is comfortable
Ask the patient to bite together on it
Remove and reseat it once to check adaptation
mcqs.explain: Any movement during setting is recorded permanently as distortion.

mcqs.q: The impression should be removed from the mouth with:
opts: A snap removal
A slow steady pull
A rocking motion from side to side
A rotating motion
mcqs.explain: An elastomer recovers best from a single rapid displacement; a slow pull leaves more permanent deformation.

mcqs.q: The final step after removing the impression is to:
opts: Clean and disinfect it
Pour the cast immediately in the surgery
Store it in water until the next day
Trim the excess material with a scalpel
mcqs.explain: Disinfection protects the laboratory staff and must precede pouring.

mcqs.q: In the putty wash technique, which tray is selected?
opts: A suitable stock tray
A custom tray
A dual-arch tray
A perforated metal tray only
mcqs.explain: The putty itself becomes the custom-fitting carrier once it has set against the teeth.

mcqs.q: How much putty is used in the putty wash technique?
opts: Two scoops, mixed with catalyst by hand
One scoop, mixed with catalyst by hand
Two scoops, mixed on a pad with a spatula
A quantity measured by weight
mcqs.explain: Manufacturer-supplied scoops give the correct proportion by volume.

mcqs.q: In the putty wash technique, the catalyst may be supplied as:
opts: Putty, paste or drops
Putty only
Paste only
A light-cured liquid
mcqs.explain: Whichever form is supplied, the mixing is done by hand.

mcqs.q: The purpose of the polyethylene spacer in the putty wash technique is to:
opts: Create a uniform channel of space for the light body wash
Prevent the putty from sticking to the tray
Speed the setting of the putty
Protect the patient's soft tissues from the putty
mcqs.explain: It reproduces the even 2–3 mm of space that a custom tray would otherwise have provided.

mcqs.q: In the putty wash technique, the tray is removed from the mouth:
opts: After initial setting of the putty
After complete setting of the putty
Before the putty begins to set
Only after the wash has also set
mcqs.explain: The spacer is then peeled off and the light body wash applied.

mcqs.q: After mixing the light body in the putty wash technique:
opts: Part is loaded in the impression syringe and the remainder is applied to the tray
All of it is loaded into the impression syringe and injected
All of it is applied to the tray and none is syringed
Half of it is discarded to avoid excessive bulk
mcqs.explain: The syringe portion is injected around the teeth, and the tray portion goes over the putty.

mcqs.q: In the putty wash technique, the retraction cord is removed:
opts: After the light body has been mixed, before injecting it
Before the putty is seated
After the final impression has been removed
Before the stock tray is selected
mcqs.explain: The teeth are washed and dried immediately before the wash is injected.

mcqs.q: The key procedural difference between the one-step and the putty wash techniques is that:
opts: The putty wash technique requires TWO seatings, the one-step requires only one
The one-step technique requires two seatings
The putty wash technique does not use a light body
The one-step technique does not use tray adhesive
mcqs.explain: In the putty wash technique the putty is set and the spacer peeled off before the wash is applied.

mcqs.q: The closed-mouth impression technique is also called the:
opts: Triple technique
Double mix technique
Single mix technique
Monophase technique
mcqs.explain: It is so called because one impression records the prepared arch, the opposing arch and the bite.

mcqs.q: In the closed-mouth technique, the impression is made while:
opts: The patient closes into the dual-arch tray in occlusion
The patient holds the mouth wide open
The operator holds the tray against the prepared arch only
The opposing arch is covered with a separating medium
mcqs.explain: The material sets with the teeth in maximum intercuspation, which is what captures the interocclusal relationship.

mcqs.q: In the optical impression, the prepared teeth are recorded by:
opts: An intraoral scanner, with no impression material at all
A light body wash in a custom tray
A putty impression that is then scanned extraorally
A photograph taken with a mirror
mcqs.explain: The whole chain — scan, design, mill — can be completed with no conventional impression or stone cast.

mcqs.q: What does the software display in colour after the opposing arch and bite have been scanned?
opts: The occlusal contacts
The shade of the adjacent teeth
The depth of the gingival sulcus
The pulp outline
mcqs.explain: Interferences can therefore be identified before the restoration is manufactured.

mcqs.q: In the CAD stage of the digital workflow:
opts: The virtual dies are sectioned, the margin is marked, and the restoration is designed on screen
The restoration is milled from a solid block of ceramic
The scan data are transmitted to the laboratory for pouring
The shade is selected electronically from a digital tab
mcqs.explain: Milling is the CAM stage that follows the CAD design.

mcqs.q: In the CAM stage, the restoration is:
opts: Cut from a solid block under water irrigation
Pressed from a wax pattern
Cast in a conventional investment
Printed layer by layer in wax
mcqs.explain: The milling unit receives the completed design file directly from the CAD software.

mcqs.q: Which is a stated advantage of the optical impression?
opts: No impression material, tray or adhesive, so no material distortion or setting error
It works equally well through blood and saliva
It captures deep subgingival margins more easily than a conventional impression
It requires no operator training
mcqs.explain: Moisture control and deep margins remain as demanding as with a conventional impression.

mcqs.q: Which is a stated disadvantage of the optical impression?
opts: High initial equipment cost
The impression cannot be reviewed until the laboratory receives it
The digital file degrades over time
A deficient area cannot be rescanned without repeating the whole scan
mcqs.explain: Immediate review and selective rescanning are in fact among its advantages.

mcqs.q: An advantage of the digital file over a conventional impression is that it:
opts: Is stored indefinitely and can be reused without the model degrading
Does not require the margin to be exposed
Eliminates the need for retraction cord
Can be read even when the field is wet
mcqs.explain: A stone cast chips and abrades with handling; a file does not.

mcqs.q: In evaluating the impression, 'Is there an area where the custom tray shows through?' is asked because:
opts: The material there was too thin to resist distortion
The adhesive was applied too thickly
The patient closed on the tray
The tray was over-extended
mcqs.explain: This is the defect that the 2–3 mm even space requirement is designed to prevent.

mcqs.q: Voids, folds or creases in an impression indicate that:
opts: The wash was disturbed or began to set before the tray was seated
The tray was too rigid
The patient's saliva was too thick
The disinfectant was too strong
mcqs.explain: This is why both viscosities must be mixed at the same time in the one-step technique.

mcqs.q: An impression in which the material has SEPARATED FROM THE TRAY must be retaken because:
opts: The adhesive failed, so the recorded position of the teeth is unreliable
The material will set too quickly
It cannot be disinfected
The laboratory cannot pour it in stone
mcqs.explain: A detached impression has moved relative to its rigid carrier, so all the recorded relationships are suspect.

mcqs.q: Which evaluation question specifically checks that the FINISH LINE has been captured?
opts: Is there an even, uninterrupted extension of material beyond the margins of the prepared teeth?
Has the material been properly mixed?
Are there any voids, folds or creases?
Has the impression material separated from the tray?
mcqs.explain: Material must extend beyond the margin for the technician to identify where the preparation ends.

mcqs.q: Streaks remaining in the set impression material indicate:
opts: An incomplete setting reaction in those areas
Contamination with saliva
That the material was over-mixed
That the tray adhesive has dissolved
mcqs.explain: 'Has the material been properly mixed?' is the first of the five evaluation questions.

mcqs.q: Which is an ideal requirement of a custom impression tray?
opts: Even space for impression material, 2–3 mm
A flexible body that adapts on seating
Extension to the prepared teeth only
A smooth internal surface with no retention
mcqs.explain: It must also be rigid, dimensionally stable, extended 3–5 mm apical to the gingival margins, and retentive for the material.

mcqs.q: A custom tray should extend apical to the gingival margins by:
opts: 3–5 mm
1 mm
10 mm
Exactly to the margin
mcqs.explain: It must include all prepared and unprepared teeth.

mcqs.q: Which is a limitation of a STOCK tray?
opts: Uneven wax space across the arch
Uniform 2–3 mm material space
Reduced polymerization shrinkage
Lower strain on removal
mcqs.explain: The excessive, uneven material thickness is what drives the shrinkage and the strain.

mcqs.q: A custom tray reduces shrinkage mainly because:
opts: Less impression material is used
The resin is more rigid
The adhesive is stronger
The tray is perforated
mcqs.explain: Shrinkage is proportional to the bulk of elastomer.

mcqs.q: Which tray material requires a monomer–polymer mix?
opts: Autopolymerizing PMMA
Light-polymerized VLC resin
Vacuum-formed thermoplastic sheet
Shellac baseplate
mcqs.explain: VLC resin is cured in a light unit with no monomer mixing.

mcqs.q: Vacuum-formed thermoplastic sheets are characterised by:
opts: Quick fabrication by heating and adapting to the cast
A monomer–polymer mixing stage
Curing in a light unit
Being the most dimensionally stable option
mcqs.explain: They are simply heated and adapted.

mcqs.q: Shellac baseplate as a tray material is described as:
opts: Rigid but less stable, with limited current use
The most widely used modern material
Light-cured and monomer-free
Vacuum-formed over the cast
mcqs.explain: It is a traditional baseplate resin.

mcqs.q: Deep undercuts are blocked out on the diagnostic cast to:
opts: Create a passive path of withdrawal so the tray does not lock on
Increase the retention of the tray
Reduce the amount of impression material needed
Allow the spacer to be omitted
mcqs.explain: Open embrasures are blocked out for the same reason.

mcqs.q: The wax spacer on a custom tray should be:
opts: 2–3 mm thick and uniform, extending 3–5 mm beyond the margins
0.5 mm thick over the prepared teeth only
5–6 mm thick for bulk strength
Applied only to the palatal surface
mcqs.explain: Uniform thickness is what produces the uniform material space.

mcqs.q: Tissue stops should be placed on:
opts: Non-prepared teeth
Prepared teeth
The soft tissue of the ridge
The palatal vault only
mcqs.explain: A stop on a prepared tooth would sit on the very surface the impression must record.

mcqs.q: How many tissue stops should be used, at minimum?
opts: Three
One
Two
Six
mcqs.explain: At least three give consistent, repeatable seating.

mcqs.q: The separating medium (tinfoil substitute) is applied to:
opts: The whole cast — the wax spacer and the exposed stone
The wax spacer only
The stone only
The fitting surface of the finished tray
mcqs.explain: It prevents the acrylic bonding to the stone so the tray lifts off cleanly.

mcqs.q: Retention holes are drilled in a custom tray to provide:
opts: Mechanical retention of the impression material
Escape vents for excess material only
A path for the adhesive to drain
A reduction in tray weight
mcqs.explain: Chemical retention comes from the adhesive; the perforations are the mechanical component.

mcqs.q: Tray adhesive should be:
opts: Matched to the impression material and applied thinly and uniformly
Applied as thickly as possible to maximise the bond
Applied only around the borders of the tray
Omitted whenever the tray has been perforated
mcqs.explain: Missing adhesive is a stated cause of material separation.

mcqs.q: Which elastomer requires immediate pouring because it releases an alcohol by-product?
opts: Condensation silicone
Addition silicone
Polyether
Polysulfide
mcqs.explain: The evaporating alcohol causes distortion and shrinkage on standing.

mcqs.q: Which elastomer offers excellent dimensional stability and high elastic recovery but needs a dry field?
opts: Addition silicone
Condensation silicone
Polysulfide
Polyether
mcqs.explain: Its hydrophobic nature is why moisture control matters.

mcqs.q: Which elastomer is inherently hydrophilic with excellent detail reproduction?
opts: Polyether
Addition silicone
Condensation silicone
Polysulfide
mcqs.explain: Hydrophilicity lets it wet a slightly moist preparation.

mcqs.q: Which elastomer has a long working time and high tear strength?
opts: Polysulfide
Addition silicone
Polyether
Condensation silicone
mcqs.explain: It also requires immediate pouring after removal.

mcqs.q: During syringe injection, the tip should be kept submerged in the material to:
opts: Prevent air entrapment
Speed up the setting reaction
Reduce the amount of material used
Improve the adhesion to the tray
mcqs.explain: A steady bead with the tip buried avoids trapped bubbles.

mcqs.q: Where should syringe injection begin?
opts: At the deepest margin point
At the most accessible buccal surface
At the incisal edge
At the adjacent unprepared tooth
mcqs.explain: The start point is then overlapped to seal the circle.

mcqs.q: While the impression sets, the tray must be:
opts: Held motionless with steady, firm pressure
Rocked gently to help adaptation
Held by the patient biting down
Released as soon as it is seated
mcqs.explain: Immobility prevents distortion and ensures accurate margins.

mcqs.q: What is the FIRST step in removing a set impression?
opts: Break the peripheral air seal
Pull firmly along the long axis
Rock the tray buccolingually
Ask the patient to open wide and bite
mcqs.explain: The vacuum must be disrupted before any traction is applied.

mcqs.q: The impression should be withdrawn:
opts: Along the long axis of the tooth, following the path of insertion
With a rocking buccolingual motion
At 45 degrees to the occlusal plane
In whatever direction is most comfortable
mcqs.explain: Rocking distorts the elastomeric impression.

mcqs.q: Which is one of the inspection criteria for a completed impression?
opts: A 360° continuous finish line on every prepared tooth
A visible tray surface through the material
A detectable separation at the margins
Drags and tears at the sulcus
mcqs.explain: The other three options are the defects being looked for.

mcqs.q: Tray show-through in an impression indicates:
opts: Insufficient material thickness over the tray
Excess adhesive was applied
The material set too slowly
The retraction cord was left in place
mcqs.explain: Ensuring no tray exposure is one of the four inspection criteria.

mcqs.q: Drags or tears in an impression indicate:
opts: Premature removal or tissue interference
Too much tray adhesive
An expired batch of catalyst
Excessive retraction time
mcqs.explain: They are the classic sign of removing before the set is complete.

mcqs.q: An impression should first be rinsed under cool running water for:
opts: 15–30 seconds
5 minutes
1 hour
No rinsing is needed
mcqs.explain: This removes saliva, blood and debris without causing distortion.

mcqs.q: Which chemical agents are recommended for disinfecting impressions?
opts: Glutaraldehyde or iodophor
Sodium hypochlorite only
Ethyl alcohol only
Hydrogen peroxide only
mcqs.explain: Both are effective against a broad spectrum of microorganisms.

mcqs.q: Why must manufacturer immersion limits be observed?
opts: Prolonged immersion can cause dimensional change
Short immersion fails to kill spores
The disinfectant loses potency over time
The tray adhesive dissolves
mcqs.explain: Over-immersion distorts the elastomer.

mcqs.q: The standard disinfection sequence is:
opts: Rinse, disinfect, rinse again, air dry before pouring
Disinfect, rinse, pour immediately
Rinse, pour, then disinfect the cast
Air dry, disinfect, pour wet
mcqs.explain: Material compatibility with the disinfectant must always be verified.

mcqs.q: A margin TEAR in an impression is most often caused by:
opts: Inadequate retraction
Moisture contamination
Missing adhesive
Premature tray removal
mcqs.explain: The finish line must be fully exposed before the material is injected.

mcqs.q: Margin VOIDS in an impression are most often caused by:
opts: Moisture contamination
Inadequate retraction
Missing adhesive
Excessive seating pressure
mcqs.explain: Moisture ruins the margin detail.

mcqs.q: Separation of the impression material from the tray indicates:
opts: Missing adhesive
Premature removal
Inadequate retraction
Moisture contamination
mcqs.explain: Adhesive must always be applied to the tray and matched to the material.

mcqs.q: In the putty-wash technique, relief space is created to:
opts: Prevent hydraulic pressure distorting the wash
Increase the bulk of the putty
Speed the setting of the light body
Improve the tray adhesive bond
mcqs.explain: Inadequate relief causes material compression and final distortion.

mcqs.q: Relief space over the putty may be created with:
opts: A plastic sheet spacer or a bur-cut relief
Additional tray adhesive
A second layer of putty
A thicker stock tray
mcqs.explain: Either method produces a controlled wash layer of uniform thickness.

mcqs.q: In the monophase (single mix) technique, the material used is:
opts: One medium-viscosity mix for both syringe and tray
Putty in the tray with a light body wash
Heavy body in the tray with light body in the syringe
A different viscosity for each arch
mcqs.explain: A single viscosity simplifies handling and one seating reduces distortion.

mcqs.q: In the dual-viscosity single-step technique, the light body is:
opts: Syringed around the margin while heavy body is loaded in the tray
Loaded in the tray while heavy body is syringed
Used alone without any tray material
Applied after the heavy body has set
mcqs.explain: Both materials are expressed simultaneously and the tray seated over the light body.

saqs.q: List the five ideal requirements of an impression tray.
saqs.a: Rigid · dimensionally stable · even space for the material, 2–3 mm · extended to include all prepared and unprepared teeth, 3–5 mm apical to the gingival margins · retentive for the material, mechanically or chemically.

list: Provide even space for the impression material — 2–3 mm
Extended to include all prepared and unprepared teeth — 3–5 mm apical to the gingival margins
Retentive for the impression material, mechanically or chemically

saqs.q: Name the four viscosities of impression material used in fixed prosthodontics.
saqs.a: Putty · heavy body · medium body · light body.

saqs.q: Compare manual and machine mixing of impression materials.
saqs.a: MANUAL — equal amounts of base and catalyst on a pad, spatulated until homogeneous; putty is dispensed with the manufacturer's scoops and kneaded between the fingers. MACHINE — prepackaged cartridges with a disposable mixing tip; advantages a homogeneous mix with fewer voids; disadvantages larger gun systems need a steadier hand to track the margin, and more waste.

head: MANUAL mixing
MACHINE mixing
rows: equal amounts of base and catalyst on a pad, spatulated until homogeneous; putty is dispensed with the manufacturer's scoops and kneaded between the fingers
prepackaged cartridges with a disposable mixing tip on the mixing tube

Advantages — a homogeneous mix with fewer voids.
Disadvantages — larger gun systems need a steadier hand to track the preparation margin, and there is more waste

saqs.q: Name the three impression techniques, and define the double mix impression.
saqs.a: 1 ONE STEP — heavy body and light body combination. 2 PUTTY WASH — two steps. 3 SINGLE MIX — medium body, for implants only. The DOUBLE MIX impression uses two viscosities — putty or heavy body with light body — and may be one step or two step.

ans.text: The DOUBLE MIX impression uses two different viscosities — putty or heavy body with light body — and may be one step or two step.

saqs.q: Describe the one-step impression technique step by step.
saqs.a: Evaluate the custom tray · apply adhesive · isolate and place retraction cord · dispense equal amounts on separate pads · mix the light body and load the syringe · at the same time mix the heavy body and load the tray · remove the cord, wash and dry · inject light body around the teeth · seat the tray and hold for the full setting time · snap removal · clean and disinfect.

steps: Evaluate the custom tray in the patient's mouth
Apply tray adhesive
Isolate the abutment teeth and place retraction cord in the sulcus
On separate pads, dispense equal amounts of base and catalyst
Mix the light body until homogeneous and load the syringe — or use an automix cartridge
At the same time, mix the heavy body and load the tray
Remove the retraction cord, wash and dry the prepared teeth
Inject the light body around the prepared teeth and the adjacent area
Seat the tray and hold it for the complete setting time
Remove with a snap removal
Clean and disinfect

saqs.q: Describe the putty wash technique step by step.
saqs.a: Select a stock tray · place retraction cord · mix two scoops of putty with catalyst by hand · load the tray · cover with a polyethylene spacer · seat and remove after initial setting · peel off the spacer · squeeze equal lengths of light body base and catalyst · mix and load syringe plus tray · remove the cord, wash and dry · inject light body and load the tray over the putty · seat the tray · remove after setting · wash, clean and disinfect.

steps: Select a suitable stock tray
Place retraction cord in the sulcus
Take two scoops of putty and mix with the catalyst by hand (putty, paste or drops)
Load the material in the tray
Cover the putty with a polyethylene spacer
Seat the tray and remove it after initial setting
Peel off the spacer
Squeeze out equal lengths of light body base and catalyst
Mix and load part in the impression syringe; the rest goes in the tray
Remove the cord, wash and dry the prepared teeth
Inject light body around the teeth and load the tray with light body over the putty
Seat the tray; after setting, remove the impression
Wash, clean and disinfect

saqs.q: What is the purpose of the polyethylene spacer, and why must the putty be removed after only initial setting?
saqs.a: The spacer stops the putty contacting the teeth, so peeling it off leaves a uniform channel for the light body wash — the same even 2–3 mm a custom tray would give. The tray comes out after INITIAL setting so the putty is firm enough to hold its form while the second stage proceeds without delay; the wash then lines the channel and records the fine detail.

rows: prevents the putty contacting the teeth — peeling it off leaves a uniform channel for the light body wash, the same even 2–3 mm a custom tray would have given
the putty is firm enough to hold its form, but the second stage proceeds without delay; the wash then lines the channel and records the fine detail

saqs.q: State the key differences between the one-step and the putty wash techniques.
saqs.a: ONE STEP — a CUSTOM tray with adhesive; heavy body in the tray, light body in the syringe; both mixed at once and the tray seated ONCE while both are unset, so they bond into a single body. PUTTY WASH — a STOCK tray; putty seated first with a spacer and removed after initial setting, the spacer peeled off, then the wash injected and the tray seated a SECOND time. Putty wash needs two seatings.

head: ONE STEP
PUTTY WASH
rows: heavy body in the tray, light body in the syringe
putty seated first with a polyethylene spacer, removed after initial setting, spacer peeled off
both mixed at the same time, tray seated ONCE while both are unset — they bond into a single body
light body wash injected and the tray seated a SECOND time — two seatings

saqs.a: A dual-arch tray is loaded on both sides and positioned over the quadrant, and the patient closes into it in maximum intercuspation. The material sets with the teeth in occlusion, so one impression records the prepared arch, the opposing arch and the interocclusal relationship together.

ans.text: A dual-arch tray is loaded on both sides and positioned over the quadrant, and the patient closes into it in maximum intercuspation. The material sets with the teeth in occlusion, so a single impression records the prepared arch, the opposing arch and the interocclusal relationship together.

saqs.q: Describe the stages of the optical (digital) impression workflow.
saqs.a: SCANNING — an intraoral scanner replaces impression material; the wand passes over the preparation and adjacent teeth and software builds a 3-D model in real time. DIGITAL MODEL — rotated, sectioned and measured on screen; scanning the opposing arch and bite shows occlusal contacts in colour. CAD DESIGN — virtual dies sectioned, margin marked on screen, contour, contacts and occlusal anatomy designed digitally. CAM MANUFACTURE — the design goes to the milling unit, which cuts the restoration from a solid block under water irrigation.

head: Stage
What happens
rows: an intraoral scanner records the prepared teeth instead of impression material — the wand passes over the preparation and adjacent teeth and software builds a three-dimensional model in real time
the virtual model can be rotated, sectioned and measured on screen; scanning the opposing arch and bite displays the occlusal contacts in colour before anything is made
virtual dies sectioned, the margin marked on screen, and contour, contacts and occlusal anatomy designed digitally
the design is sent to the milling unit, which cuts the restoration from a solid block under water irrigation

saqs.q: Give the advantages and disadvantages of the optical (digital) impression.
saqs.a: ADVANTAGES — no material, tray or adhesive, so no distortion, tearing or setting error; greater comfort, no gagging or taste; immediate review and rescanning of a deficient area; no disinfection, packing or postage; the file is stored indefinitely and never degrades. DISADVANTAGES — high initial cost; a learning curve; it still cannot read through blood or saliva, so the field must be dry and the margin exposed; deep subgingival margins and long edentulous spans remain difficult; and a hardware or software failure stops the workflow.

saqs.q: List the five questions used to evaluate a completed impression, and state what each is testing.
saqs.a: 1 Properly mixed? — streaks mean an incomplete setting reaction. 2 Tray showing through? — the material there was too thin to resist distortion. 3 Voids, folds or creases? — the wash was disturbed, or began to set before seating. 4 Even uninterrupted extension beyond the margins? — if not, the finish line is not captured. 5 Separated from the tray? — the adhesive failed, so the recorded position is unreliable. Any one is a reason to retake.

saqs.q: Why is a custom tray preferred over a stock tray?
saqs.a: STOCK TRAY LIMITATIONS — uneven wax space across the arch, excessive material thickness, higher polymerization shrinkage, and increased strain on tray removal. CUSTOM TRAY ADVANTAGES — a uniform 2–3 mm material space, reduced shrinkage from less material, lower strain which facilitates removal, and better seating which enhances accuracy. Custom trays therefore optimize impression accuracy.

saqs.q: Outline the steps of fabricating a custom acrylic tray on a diagnostic cast.
saqs.a: CAST PREPARATION — block out deep undercuts and open embrasures to create a passive path of withdrawal, using diagnostic plaster or stone. SPACER — outline the tray border, apply a uniform 2–3 mm wax spacer extending 3–5 mm beyond the margins, and cut the stop windows cleanly. STOPS — place at least three tissue stops on non-prepared teeth to orient the seating and maintain the uniform space. SEPARATING MEDIUM — apply a tinfoil substitute over the whole cast, covering wax and exposed stone, and let it dry. FABRICATION — mix PMMA monomer and polymer to a doughy, tack-free mass, form a uniform 2–3 mm sheet, adapt it over the spacer, add a strong rigid handle reinforced at the junction, and allow complete polymerization. FINISHING — trim sharp borders, smooth the acrylic, drill evenly spaced retention holes, and apply a thin uniform layer of tray adhesive matched to the impression material.

steps: Cast preparation — block out deep undercuts and open embrasures for a passive path of withdrawal
Spacer — outline the tray border; uniform 2–3 mm wax spacer extending 3–5 mm beyond the margins; cut the stop windows
Stops — at least three, on non-prepared teeth
Separating medium — tinfoil substitute over the whole cast, wax and exposed stone, dried completely
Fabrication — mix PMMA to a doughy, tack-free mass; form a uniform 2–3 mm sheet; adapt over the spacer; add a strong rigid handle; allow complete polymerization
Finishing — trim sharp borders · smooth the acrylic · drill retention holes · apply tray adhesive matched to the material

saqs.q: Classify the four elastomeric impression materials.
saqs.a: POLYSULFIDE — long working time and high tear strength, but requires immediate pouring after removal. CONDENSATION SILICONE — releases an alcohol by-product during setting, so pour immediately to prevent distortion and shrinkage. ADDITION SILICONE — excellent dimensional stability and high elastic recovery, but requires a dry field. POLYETHER — inherently hydrophilic with excellent detail reproduction.

saqs.q: Describe the correct seating and removal of an impression.
saqs.a: SEATING — seat the tray with steady, firm pressure, hold it motionless and completely stable while the material sets, prevent any patient bite force, and confirm the material has fully polymerized before removal; immobility prevents distortion and ensures accurate margins. REMOVAL — first break the peripheral air seal to disrupt the vacuum before any traction, then pull along the long axis of the tooth following the path of insertion exactly, avoiding rocking which distorts the elastomeric impression, and inspect the impression immediately for margins, voids and adhesion. Premature removal or rocking causes distortion.

steps: Break the peripheral air seal — disrupt the vacuum before any traction
Pull along the tooth long axis, following the path of insertion exactly
Avoid rocking — it distorts the elastomeric impression
Inspect immediately — margins, voids and adhesion

saqs.q: Give the inspection criteria for a completed impression and the disinfection protocol.
saqs.a: INSPECTION — a 360° continuous finish line on every prepared tooth; no surface voids, bubbles or defects on the prepared surfaces; a firm tray-material bond with no separation at the margins; and no tray show-through. Drags or tears indicate premature removal or tissue interference. DISINFECTION — rinse immediately under cool running water for 15–30 seconds to remove saliva, blood and debris without distortion; spray or immerse using a solution compatible with the material; glutaraldehyde or iodophor are the recommended agents; and follow the manufacturer's immersion limits, since prolonged immersion causes dimensional change. The standard protocol is rinse, disinfect, rinse again, air dry before pouring.

saqs.q: List the common impression failures with their mechanisms, and the cautions that prevent them.
saqs.a: MARGIN TEAR — inadequate retraction. MARGIN VOIDS — moisture contamination. MATERIAL SEPARATION — missing adhesive. DISTORTION — premature tray removal. The cautions are: retraction, to expose the finish line fully; a dry field, since moisture ruins margins; adhesive, always applied to the tray; setting time, holding the tray motionless; and inspection of a 360° finish line before pouring.
